title: Strings: raw and interpreted literals, immutability and UTF-8

videos.script: Lesson 8 ended with one word and three lengths. This lesson is about the type that word lives in, the string. {{literals}} It starts with how you write one. Go has two kinds of string literal. In double quotes, a backslash starts an escape. In backquotes, nothing does. You will see a Windows path that compiles, passes go vet, and prints a newline in the middle. {{immutable}} Then what a string is underneath. Its bytes never change after it is made. A string value is just a pointer and a length, so taking part of a string copies nothing. Adding two strings copies everything, and in a loop that gets slow very fast. {{builder}} One program takes almost four seconds, the other three milliseconds, and they print the same thing. {{utf8}} Last, indexing. s of three is a byte, not a character, and cutting a string in the wrong place leaves half a letter behind. The unicode slash utf8 package tells you when that has happened.
